chunks.content: Rising rates of US perinatal morbidity and mortality have been and remain a critical public health concern. Of the 800 to 1200 annual United States (US) maternal deaths, 80% are preventable. These deaths occur in a population that is young and healthy enough to become pregnant, with an average age of 27 years among first pregnancies. Compared with similarly resourced countries, the United States ranks 55th in the world for adverse perinatal outcomes despite spending the most worldwide on perinatal care. This is compounded by sharp health inequities, with birth outcomes disproportionately worse among Black and/or Indigenous identified people compared with their White counterparts. Overall, US health systems too often fail to protect childbearing women, especially those who identify as racial/ethnic minorities. Perinatal provider burnout is high among midwives and obstetricians, , and fewer medical and nursing students are choosing to specialize in childbearing care. In addition, there is a widening of US maternity care deserts, , defined as “any county without a hospital or birthing center offering obstetric care and without any obstetric provider.” Such deserts are more prevalent in rural counties, and more than half (51%) of all US rural counties lack a facility that provides perinatal care; 47% lack an obstetrician, 62% lack a midwife, and 36% lack any perinatal care provider. Adverse health outcomes are worse in maternity care deserts. There are many health system differences between the United States and countries reporting better perinatal outcomes, such as paid parental leave and extended postpartum care. , Another prominent health system difference that has received less attention relates to the size of the midwifery workforce and integration of midwives within perinatal care services. Midwives are perinatal providers trained to care for the majority (approximately 85%) of pregnant women, characterized as “low risk.” Most high-income countries rely on midwives to deliver the majority of perinatal care, with consultation or transfer to physician care as needed based on patient risk status. For example, the Swedish perinatal care workforce is composed of 12 obstetricians and 69 midwives per 1000 births versus the US perinatal care workforce with 12 obstetricians and 4 midwives per 1000 births. Of note, maternal deaths in Sweden are 3/100,000 live births in comparison to 22/100,000 live births in the United States. In the United Kingdom and Norway, midwives provide the majority of perinatal care; both countries report maternal morbidity and mortality rates much lower than the United States. Altogether, midwifery workforce expansion and integration are underexplored opportunities to improve US perinatal outcomes. The purpose of this review is to synthesize literature and state policy regarding the expansion and integration of midwifery care as a promising health systems solution to improving US perinatal outcomes. We define “midwife” and “midwifery model of care” as well as describe the US midwifery workforce and outcomes research. We delineate 6 historical, structural, or discriminatory barriers to US midwifery workforce expansion and integration. Finally, we provide opportunities to overcome these barriers with recommendations for implementation. Given that the majority, but not all, who become pregnant and birth in the United States identify as a woman, we center female-gendered terms in describing our population of interest but periodically use nongendered terms in recognition of childbearing gender minorities. <italic toggle="yes">WHO IS A MIDWIFE?</italic> DEFINING MIDWIFERY IN THE UNITED STATES AND INTERNATIONALLY The International Confederation of Midwives (ICM) defines a midwife as “…a person who has successfully completed a midwifery education programme based on the ICM Essential Competencies for Midwifery Practice and the framework of the ICM Global Standards for Midwifery Education, recognized in the country where it is located; who has acquired the requisite qualifications to be registered and/or legally licensed to practice midwifery and use the title ‘midwife,’ and who demonstrates competency in the scope of practice of the midwife.” US midwifery training, certification, and licensure engage varying pathways, professional titles, and scopes of practice. Certified nurse-midwives (CNMs) and certified midwives (CMs) deliver more than 90% of US midwifery care; CNMs/CMs are trained in educational programs that align with ICM midwifery definition and care standards. CNM/CM training occurs in programs accredited by the US Department of Education recognized Accreditation Commission for Midwifery Education, predominantly within university-based schools of nursing and/or medicine (two programs are in colleges of health professions). After passing clinical and didactic training requirements, CNM/CMs are certified by the American Midwifery Certification Board (AMCB) and are licensed at the state level, typically within boards of nursing or medicine. The majority (99%) of AMCB-CMs are CNMs, and 1% are CMs. CNMs are recognized and licensed in every state as well as the District of Columbia, and CMs are currently recognized and licensed in 12 states and the District of Columbia. The majority (99%) of AMCB-CMs are CNMs, and 1% are CMs. CNMs are recognized and licensed in every state as well as the District of Columbia, and CMs are currently recognized and licensed in 12 states and the District of Columbia. The majority (94%) of CNM/CM care is provided within hospital systems. , , Certified professional midwives (CPMs) provide nearly all community setting (home birth and birth center) perinatal care and compose 9.1% of the overall US midwifery workforce. The pathways of CPM education, certification, and licensure are distinct from the aforementioned AMCB pathway. CPM education in programs accredited by the Midwifery Education Accreditation Council meets ICM standards. CPM education in apprenticeship-based programs that are not Midwifery Education Accreditation Council–accredited does not meet ICM standards. CPM training generally occurs outside of university and schools of nursing and medicine systems and engages distinct state licensure processes. A third midwifery path is through the unlicensed apprenticeship route, or traditional midwives. Traditional midwives attend a very small percent of US home births. Having three US midwifery pathways, which vary in training, certification, licensure, and predominant care setting, has contributed to interprofessional and public confusion about the midwifery profession, scope of practice, and care setting. This review will focus on the largest sector (>90%) of the US midwifery workforce, AMBC-certified CNMs/CMs, who attended approximately 11% of all US births in 2022. Use of the term “midwife” for the remainder or this article refers to AMCB-certified CNM/CMs, unless otherwise noted. WHAT IS THE MIDWIFERY MODEL OF CARE? Midwives are master’s degree or doctorally trained, advanced practice experts in low-risk, person-centered sexual and reproductive health care, including well-woman care, family planning, perinatal care (antepartum, intrapartum, and postpartum), preconception care, lactation support, and perimenopausal/menopausal care. With additional training, midwives also perform procedures such as endometrial biopsy, colposcopy, punch biopsy, abortion care, first assist for cesarean birth, and circumcision. The midwifery model of care in all clinical applications prioritizes promotion of optimal physical, emotional, and social outcomes and emphasizes patient autonomy and empowerment, person-centered and respectful care, and conservative use of interventions. , The Quality Maternal and Newborn Care (QMNC) framework, developed in 2014 as part of a Lancet series on midwifery care, articulates a Midwifery Model of Care with 3 categories: ( a ) education, information, and health promotion; ( b ) assessment, screening, and care planning; and ( c ) promotion of normal processes, prevention of complications, as well as the initial steps of caring for those with complications, specifically first-line management of complications, including accurate recognition of risk and expedient consultation or transfer of care to obstetricians or perinatologists. The QMNC framework is further articulated by the values (“respect, communication, community knowledge and understanding; care tailored towards women’s circumstances and needs”) and philosophy (“optimizing biological, psychological, social and cultural processes; strengthening women’s capabilities; expectant management, using interventions only when indicated”), echoing prior research and aligning with a recent US midwifery care concept analysis. These aspects of the QMNC framework align with how the midwifery practice is defined: “skilled, knowledgeable, and compassionate care for childbearing women, newborn infants, and families across the continuum throughout prepregnancy, pregnancy, birth, postpartum, and the early weeks of life. Core characteristics include optimizing normal biological, psychological, social, and cultural processes of reproduction and early life; timely prevention and management of complications; consultation with and referral to other services; respect for women’s individual circumstances and views; and working in partnership with women to strengthen women’s own capabilities to care for themselves and their families.” (p1130) IS MIDWIFERY CARE SAFE? Decades of research characterize midwifery care as safe. In a large review of 17 studies that included randomized subjects (n = 18,533) in 5 non-US countries, midwifery continuity of care models were associated with higher rates of safe spontaneous vaginal birth and lower rates of cesarean birth when compared with other models of care. These findings are consistent with studies of US birthing women cared for by midwives – and with health systems that integrate midwifery care. – Critique of midwifery care outcomes frequently centers on concerns about research bias related to midwifery versus obstetrician patient risk status and self-selection of midwifery care—which are both important considerations. Health systems research offers important insight on these concerns. For example, Rosenstein et al (2015) studied 4884 laboring women with a pre/post study design to assess outcomes associated with a community hospital policy change from a private practice model to a midwifery and laborist model. Health systems research offers important insight on these concerns. For example, Rosenstein et al (2015) studied 4884 laboring women with a pre/post study design to assess outcomes associated with a community hospital policy change from a private practice model to a midwifery and laborist model. Patients in this system did not choose their attending providers, and their risk status was constant, so the only factor that changed was the intrapartum care team model. This change dropped the primary cesarean birth rate from 31.7% to 25.0% and increased the vaginal birth after cesarean rate from 13.3% to 22.4%. Similar midwifery care health systems patterns have been noted in more recent research. – Birthing women attended by midwives are less likely to use anesthesia and oxytocin for augmentation and induction and have better outcomes for certain measures (eg, patient satisfaction, preterm birth/small for gestational age infants, and breastfeeding initiation and duration) when compared with birthing women with the same health risks but attended by obstetricians. , – These improved outcomes may be related to conservative use of interventions and promotion of birth as a normal physiologic process. , , Further, there is evidence that midwifery care is associated with lower resource use and costs. , – Despite this evidence, the US midwifery model and scope of care is frequently misunderstood and not commonly integrated, normalized, or sustained in domestic perinatal care systems. , , Increasing access to and utilization of midwifery care has not been widely examined as a meaningful health systems solution to improving US perinatal care outcomes. BARRIERS TO ACCESS AND UTILIZATION OF MIDWIFERY CARE Six factors have had a chilling effect on the expansion and wider integration of midwives into the US perinatal workforce: (1) limited midwifery workforce development, (2) historical roots of systemic racism and dismantling of the midwifery workforce, (3) invisibility of midwifery care in key perinatal data, (4) inequitable reimbursement rates, (5) regulatory and legislative restrictions to accessing midwifery care, and (6) and discriminatory hospital policies. Limited Workforce Development A key barrier to expanding access to US midwifery care is a lack of state and federal funding for midwifery education and training. Whereas federal graduate medical education funds support US medical training, no parallel fund for midwifery training exists. Compared with the 195 US medical schools that educate obstetricians-gynecologists or MD/doctor of philosophy (PhD) trainees, there are 46 CNM/CM midwifery educational programs that culminate in either master's (master of science in nursing) or doctoral (doctor of nursing practice [DNP], or doctor of midwifery [PhD]) degrees; several of these programs also confer master of science or a master of science in midwifery degrees. It is estimated that approximately 11% of midwives in the United States hold a doctoral degree, predominantly the DNP. There are 13 states without midwifery education programs despite each state having at least one school of nursing (Idaho [ID], Wyoming [WY], North Dakota [ND], South Dakota [SD], Missouri [MO], Indiana [IN], Oklahoma [OK], Alaska [AK], Mississippi [MS], West Virginia [WV], Vermont [VT], New Hampshire [NH], Maine [ME]). One of the greatest limiting factors to the growth of the midwifery workforce is the lack of funds to pay midwifery preceptors for time devoted to clinical teaching, resulting in a limited number of preceptors willing to volunteer their time. Of midwifery program applicants who meet standards for midwifery education programs admission, a limited number are admitted due to the shortage of clinical preceptors. In addition to the limited number and regional distribution of midwifery education programs and compensation for preceptor effort, graduate midwifery education is expensive and rarely buffered by financial support. For example, the most expensive nurse-midwifery program in the United States costs $2550 per credit hour, whereas the least expensive costs $240 per credit hour, with programs varying in length from 2 to 3 years. Only 38% of nurse-midwifery students receive scholarship or grants for their education, with many relying on loans that must be paid back upon graduation. This contrasts with 64% of medical students who reported receiving financial aid (scholarships, grants, and/or stipends) in 2024. To pursue their education, more than half of midwifery students work at least 20 hours per week and attend school part time, , providing at least 50% of their household incomes. , These realities place a significant time constraint and financial burden on midwifery students and graduates that further influence financial decisions regarding where to practice upon graduation. Historic Racism and Dismantling of the Midwifery Workforce In the 19th and early 20th centuries, US midwifery was nearly eradicated by the spread of disinformation, fueled by classism, sexism, and racism. For example, midwifery care at this time was characterized as “poor quality” and “dangerous.” Health systems moved most births into hospitals at a time when women were just beginning to enter the medical profession and thus rarely in the hospital setting. The 1910 Flexner Report highlighted the lack of standardization and rigor in medical education and called for the closure of most US medical schools, with only a handful of well-funded schools remaining open—reshaping class-based determination of who provides childbearing care. These recommendations were widely accepted and led to the consolidation of educational, class, and male-dominated influence and power within medicine. As a result, medical schools became the domain of upper middle-class White men who had previously been excluded from sexual and reproductive health and birth care. The need to train physicians in obstetrics increased pressure to move birth away from midwives and home settings to hospitals with physician supervision. Given the preponderance of male physicians at this time, these changes resulted in systematically moving childbearing care out of women’s domain in the community and into men’s domain in the hospital. Institutional racism also played a key role in undermining traditional US midwifery care models. White public health nurses, nurse-midwives, and obstetricians began to dominate care delivery at this time, which became a means to suppress, marginalize, or eliminate the longstanding Black, Indigenous, and immigrant midwifery workforces. This trend was amplified in 1921 with the federal Sheppard-Towner Act. Designed to address the high maternal and infant mortality rate, this Act placed erroneous blame on Black, Indigenous, and immigrant midwives (eg, no evidence was offered to support the claim that midwives were “slovenly, immoral, drunken, promiscuous, and perverse” ). The Sheppard-Towner Act catalyzed development of a federally funded public health workforce made up nearly exclusively of White public health nurses and nurse-midwives. The purposeful early 20th-century decimation of Black, Indigenous, and immigrant midwives continues to influence contemporary childbearing care patterns in the United States. Disinformation and professional competition remain barriers to acceptance and integration of midwives into the health care system, as well as a lack of diversity in the midwifery workforce. In 2023, the AMCB reported that 84.2% of the midwifery workforce identified racially as White, 7.7% as Black or African American, 0.6% as American Indian or Alaskan Native, 0.2% as Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander, and 1.8% as Asian. Only 5.2% of the workforce ethnically identified as Latina/Latino. The rest of the workforce identified as other race or multiple races or chose not to respond. There are strong arguments to diversify the midwifery workforce. , The White midwifery workforce is implicated with reported racial discrimination in providing patient care. One large prospective cohort study found that only 37% of Black people report satisfaction with their pregnancy care and birth experience, and 40.1% of Black; 36.6% of Hispanic; 31.4% of American Indian, Alaska Native, Pacific Islander, or Native Hawaiian; and 39.4% of multiracial people report experiences of discrimination during the perinatal period. Multiple studies indicate that birthing people of color prefer providers from their race and/or culture, termed racially/ethnically concordant care, and have significantly better perinatal outcomes with concordant care. – Invisibility in Birth Certificate Data A critical barrier to expansion and integration of the US midwifery workforce is the underreporting of midwife-attended births in state vital statistics, which are routinely miscoded as physician-attended births. Several studies have found vital statistics rates underreporting midwife-attended births ranging from 19% to 65%. – These errors are likely driven by the widely varying qualifications, training, and expertise of hospital staff who collect birth certificate data. – Underreporting of midwifery care also may be due to the presence of more than one provider at the birth (midwife and physician) or birth certificate staff assuming that midwives are not allowed to provide care independent of physician oversight. Although vital statistics accuracy is ultimately the responsibility of the health care provider, very few are trained to evaluate these data or empowered with time and guidance to correct these errors. The underreporting of midwifery care attribution in vital statistics has adverse fiscal, research, and health policy ramifications. Although vital statistics accuracy is ultimately the responsibility of the health care provider, very few are trained to evaluate these data or empowered with time and guidance to correct these errors. The underreporting of midwifery care attribution in vital statistics has adverse fiscal, research, and health policy ramifications. First, inaccurately assigning births to physicians when care was delivered by midwives leads to invisibility of midwifery care and its growth (or decline) over time in routinely collected data. Second, because birth certificates serve as a rich data source to evaluate perinatal outcomes, underreporting makes it difficult for researchers and policymakers to study health systems outcomes and contributions, or shortcomings, of midwifery care. Finally, if birth certificate data are used for billing of services, errors in care attribution may also lead to inaccurate or limited reimbursement for midwifery services. Inequitable Reimbursement Reimbursement rates for midwifery services under Medicaid and private insurances vary significantly state to state. , , More than 40% of all US births are covered by Medicaid, and Medicaid payment patterns routinely set the pace for both public and private payment structures. In 31 states, Medicaid reimburses for midwifery services at the same rate as physician services; however, in 29 states, midwifery reimbursement rates are lower, ranging from 75% to 97%, of the physician reimbursement rate for the same services. In contrast, Medicare reimbursement rates for Part B services are equitable between CNMs and physicians. These state-level Medicaid payment variations by provider type for the same work negatively impact midwifery workforce sustainability. A review of practice costs identified that, in 24 of the 50 states, the actual costs of providing perinatal care exceed the payment received by midwives. Shifting Medicaid reimbursement rates such that equal pay for equal work is standard may also incentivize hospitals to continue to provide perinatal care, decreasing the number of maternity care deserts. This is particularly urgent in rural areas of the United States, where midwives are more likely to practice compared with physicians. States with large rural populations are particularly impacted by these variations in Medicaid payment, with one example described below. MIDWIFERY CARE IN ALABAMA: A CASE STUDY Jaya is a 23-year-old pregnant woman living in rural Sumter County in the Black Belt of Alabama (AL). This is her first pregnancy, and she is currently 35 weeks pregnant. Because she has Medicaid insurance, Jaya must drive over an hour to access care by a provider who accepts this insurance. However, Jaya missed her 34-week visit due to lack of transportation. She could not afford the repair needed on her car and was not able to arrange her work schedule to be off when a ride from a friend was available. Jaya receives a telephone call from the clinic nurse after her missed appointment and shares she is having severe headaches and blurry vision. The nurse is concerned about these symptoms and asks Jaya to immediately go to a nearby emergency room. Jaya is hesitant because she was instructed to go to the emergency room 2 weeks earlier due to the same symptoms, and in this visit, the medical team checked the baby’s heartbeat, gave her Tylenol, and sent her home. Jaya asks if she could have a telehealth appointment with her provider due to lack of transportation but is declined because her insurance will not cover telehealth visits. Jaya decides to rest at home. She is later found unresponsive and is air-lifted to Birmingham, where she undergoes an emergency cesarean birth after having a seizure on the flight. This case highlights several policy and structural barriers contributing to perinatal morbidity and mortality in AL. The prevalence of maternity care deserts has expanded; in AL, 28% of people do not have access to a birthing facility within a 30-minute drive, which is significantly higher compared with other states. AL midwives are reimbursed at 80% under Medicaid as compared with physicians, which contributes to challenges in sustaining and growing the AL midwifery workforce. Consequently, midwives are more likely to practice in neighboring states. In addition, midwives are not well integrated into AL health systems. In 2024, 53 midwives were licensed in the state, yet less than half attended births due to state-level practice barriers. Regulatory and Legislative Restrictions States are responsible for licensing midwives and determining what services they can provide. Restrictions in midwifery practice are rooted in state regulatory and legislative laws. , , , – In 25 states and the District of Columbia, midwives can practice independently, without restrictions to their licensure or prescriptive authority. However, access to midwifery care is limited in the other 25 states. , , One example of a state restriction is a mandate that midwives must secure a written contractual agreement with a physician to be licensed to provide or obtain prescriptive authority. This dependence on a physician’s willingness to legally contract with midwives leads to professional, financial, geographic, philosophical, and medicolegal constraints. – These circumstances deeply impact US midwifery workforce development and sustainability, driving issues such as challenging interprofessional dynamics, negative professional practice climate, and barriers to accepting midwifery students for clinical training. , , Recent research signals that negative practice climate, not heavy workloads, is the leading reason for midwives’ dissatisfaction with work and intent to leave their position. Legislative restrictions that tether midwifery practice to physician practice lack evidence of public benefit, increase vicarious liability and unnecessary oversight responsibility, and are inefficient and costly for midwives, physicians, patients, and the health care system at large. , – Restrictions also create an environment in which the supply of midwives is dependent on physician demand instead of patient demand for midwifery care. , , When a midwife’s ability to practice or prescribe medications is dependent on a written physician agreement and contractual relationship, restraint of trade and anticompetition often coexist. , , In some areas, multiple midwives rely on one physician to practice or prescribe. Such contractual agreements also create complexity for physicians who may feel torn between desire to support midwifery access and anxiety about perceived or real liability for midwifery care in which they are not involved or only indirectly involved. , When a contracting physician moves or retires, midwives may be unable to secure a contractual agreement with a new physician. In this scenario, the midwives may be forced to move or close their practice, compounding access issues to perinatal care for that community. Regulatory and legislative restrictions to midwifery practice also shape financial considerations and the accuracy of vital statistics. For example, in the 25 states where a midwife’s practice is tethered to a collaborating physician’s practice, the physician’s name is routinely embedded in billing and in care documentation even if that physician never directly provided cared for the patient. , , These factors add to physician anxiety about contracting with midwives as well as confusion about who delivered the care, errors in vital statistics, and billing misattribution. Midwifery practice restrictions contribute to the growing issue of US maternity care deserts. , , , , , A larger proportion of counties in practice-restricted states lack a midwife (61%) compared with those with independent midwifery practice (54%). , Of US counties that do not have an obstetrician, independent midwifery licensure is associated with improved access to care. In states with autonomous midwifery practice, counties without an obstetrician are twice as likely to have midwives (10%), whereas in restricted states, half as many counties without an obstetrician have midwives (5%). There are also a larger proportion of midwives in counties in independent practice states that have obstetricians (69%) and hospitals (72%) compared with those in states with restrictions (55% and 61%, respectively). Some states have passed individual “carve-out” laws to support midwifery practice. However, these are piecemeal responses to midwifery care regulation work efficiency challenges that bypass possible policy advances to promote more autonomous midwifery practices, appropriately based on education, training, and national certification—which do not rely on physician contractual obligations, time, or effort. , State practice restrictions also lead to care delivery “workarounds,” such as physicians signing blank prescription forms for a midwife colleague such that they can expediently prescribe commonly used medications (eg, contraception, antibiotics, prenatal vitamins) in busy perinatal care settings. Considered collectively, these circumstances maintain convoluted and varying midwifery care regulatory structures and practice patterns by state that add to overall midwifery workforce and health care integration challenges and compound general confusion about US midwifery care. NJ’s experience with restrictions to independent midwifery licensure and prescriptive authority is described below. MIDWIFERY CARE IN NJ: 3 CASE STUDIES Midwife A.M. has worked over 2 decades at a small NJ community birth center. She has been struggling to find a collaborating physician for the past 2 years, with each relationship secured becoming short-lived due to evolving needs and employment among her consulting obstetricians. Despite previously precepting midwifery students, A.M. no longer volunteers in this capacity as her ability to practice is tenuous and her health setting and physician partners are not incentivized to advance midwifery training. Midwife K.L. was caring for a patient who was diagnosed with syphilis in the antepartum period and appropriately consulted with an infectious disease specialist. Her obstetrician-gynecologist colleague, overhearing the conversation about her management plan, cavalierly replied that he was comfortable continuing to allow the midwife to care for the patient. In a similar instance, a newly hired physician was called by the nursing staff to see a patient in obstetric triage unit. Rather than leaving her call room to evaluate the patient, the new physician called midwife C.M. and told her that because the new physician needed to rest, the midwife should assess the patient and then call her to appraise her of the patient’s status. This same physician commented at a monthly department meeting that the midwives in the hospital were so competent, they were like “super-residents.” According to state and hospital policies, the individual physicians at this hospital have no oversight over these midwives as they are hospital employees and colleagues. However, NJ state policies regarding collaborative agreements perpetuate the perception that any physician in the health care system is overseeing any midwife working at the same time in the same system. Rather than interprofessional collegiality and team-based care, a hierarchy culture negatively influences midwives’ morale. Two of the above mentioned midwives in this case have since left these NJ hospital systems to work in states with independent midwifery practice authority. These NJ cases highlight several restrictive state regulatory policies contributing to midwifery practices and workforce burnout. Although midwives in NJ receive 100% of the fee a physician receives under Medicaid, and hospitals may allow midwives on medical staff, according to regulations promulgated by the NJ Board of Medical Examiners, midwives have a limited license to practice and must have specific guidelines approved by a consulting physician. The Medicaid pay parity does not extend to other payers, including Medicaid MCOs and private insurance. In addition, according to NJ state legislation, a midwife must have a collaborative agreement, including standing orders and practice protocols, to obtain prescriptive authority. Practice restrictions mandating tethered midwifery and physician care routinely create barriers to where in NJ midwives provide care. While a significant proportion at each NJ hospital’s births may be attended by midwives, most midwives in the state do not have voting privileges regarding departmental decisions, nor can they advance to departmental leadership. This impacts their ability to weigh in on, for example, whether to train midwifery students, have midwives as speakers at grand rounds, or move forward with policies that impede or facilitate use of a midwifery model of care for risk-appropriate patients. Ultimately, this lack of voice compounds a sense of powerlessness in the hospital setting and burnout, thereby decreasing access and utilization of midwifery care. Discriminatory Hospital Policies The final barrier to expansion of midwifery care relates to the predominance of hospital policies barring midwives from participation on par with physicians and/or attending status. The majority (96%) of states allow hospitals to restrict midwives’ agency in hospital governance by barring midwives’ application for full medical staff appointments. , , This creates hospital governance and leadership structures as well as cultural norms in which midwifery care practices are marginalized or truncated. The majority (96%) of states allow hospitals to restrict midwives’ agency in hospital governance by barring midwives’ application for full medical staff appointments. , , This creates hospital governance and leadership structures as well as cultural norms in which midwifery care practices are marginalized or truncated. Barring midwives from full health system participation and representation also negatively impacts the practice climate for midwives. , Further, when midwives have no agency within their hospital systems, these systems are unlikely to be aware of, let alone advocate for, opportunities to boost and/or retain the midwifery workforce. Implications that 96% of states allow hospitals to restrict midwives from due process in application for full medical staff appointments with voting rights are far reaching. For example, some systems force midwives to offer physician care models, which contributes to midwifery workforce burnout, particularly when there is incongruence between midwifery best practices and hospital practice policies. Midwifery training emphasizes the importance of patience with labor duration and continuous support of laboring women, both practices associated with improved outcomes. Hospitals employing midwives may be unaware of these benefits, minimize these benefits, and/or create care systems preventing these kinds of care practices—issues that cannot easily be addressed when midwives are not attendings, with full medical staff appointments and voting rights, in the given hospital system. When the US midwifery workforce is required to practice in systems where the midwifery philosophy and/or model of care is hard to realize, these midwives may choose alternative employment. Midwives are qualified via education and national certification to admit laboring patients to the hospital setting, yet only 2 states (New Mexico [NM] and Oregon [OR]) and the District of Columbia have laws that specifically protect midwives’ admission privileges. , , In 31 states, the law permits, but does not require, that hospitals allow midwives to admit their own patients to the hospital. In 16 states, the law prohibits hospitals from allowing midwives to admit their own patients, thereby requiring physicians to perform this task that midwives are educated to accomplish and would perform in states without restrictions. In some restricted states, regulations stipulate that physician colleagues must cosign midwives’ hospital admission orders or document their own physical examination of the midwife’s patient, creating a situation where two perinatal providers trained and licensed for the same tasks are forced to duplicate work. Elimination of workforce redundancy would lead to increased efficiencies that would decrease costs and risks for medical errors while improving access to perinatal and reproductive care services. NM, OR, and the District of Columbia also have laws requiring hospitals that allow midwives the right to apply and be considered on the merits of their application for full medical staff appointments with voting rights. NM and OR have some of the highest rates of key midwifery workforce indicators in the United States. NM has 9.9 midwives per 1000 births in the state; 24% of all births (32% of vaginal births) are midwife-attended. OR has 10 midwives per 1000 births in the state; 21% of all births (30% of vaginal births) are midwife-attended. Although not asserting causality, OR and NM have some of the best perinatal outcomes in the United States. In contrast, Nevada (NV) has only 2 midwives per 1000 births, well below the minimum 6 per 1000 recommended by the World Health Organization; only 6% of all births (9% of vaginal births) in NV are midwife-attended. NV’s experience with discriminatory hospital policies is described below. MIDWIFERY CARE IN NV: A CASE STUDY ​ NV has one of the smallest midwifery workforces in the country, reflecting the impact of historic restrictions. Midwives in NV have been licensed for independent practice since 2013, but several discriminatory policies have limited growth of the midwifery workforce. Up until 2023, the statute governing hospital licensing only allowed physicians to admit patients. The passage of SB 146 (NV 2023) removed the state prohibition against midwives independently admitting their own patients, but did not require hospitals to provide due process to midwives applying for privileges nor grant them membership on medical staff with voting rights. Thus, despite removal of these barriers at the regulatory and legislative level, many hospital bylaws maintain antiquated requirements that midwives have a physician cosign their charts or categorically deny midwives admitting privileges without evidence of need or rationale. Additionally, Medicaid reimbursement for care provided by midwives recently increased from 75% to 100% of the physical schedule by statute SB 342 (NV 2021). Elena prefers to see a midwife for her prenatal visits, birth, and postpartum care, but liked knowing an obstetrician would be available if needed. She was delighted to learn the practice had hired additional midwives, making it easier to schedule an appointment with them. The obstetrician-owner of the collaborative practice had been working for three years to hire more midwives. They are pleased the practice now has multiple midwives providing care; however, the practice has encountered new challenges that limit the midwives’ ability to contribute to the practice to the full extent of their education and national certification. The practice is part of a community laborist service to ensure there are always two providers on-site; however, midwives in NV are not allowed to serve as laborist, resulting in the obstetricians bearing the full burden for providing laborist services. In a second example, S.P. is the lead midwife at another busy collaborative midwife and obstetrician practice. Consumer demand for the midwifery service has grown over the past four years. S.P. expected the recently increased Medicaid reimbursement rates for care provided by midwives, from 75% to 100% of the physician fee schedule, would make it easier for the practice to continue to hire more midwives and expand the popular service model. Instead, the practice now feels at risk because the hospital laborists, who routinely provide backup for the obstetricians in the collaborative practice, have said they will no longer provide backup for the midwives when the practice obstetrician is unavailable. These examples highlight that even in a state with autonomous midwifery regulation and full Medicaid reimbursement, midwives still face discriminatory policies and culture at the state and hospital levels. These barriers to full integration of midwifery-led care have a negative impact on already limited access to essential perinatal and reproductive health care services. In the first case, the exclusion of midwives from the laborist pool results in an excessive and unnecessary burden on the obstetric workforce. Including midwives in the laborist pool would allow both obstetrician-obstetrician and midwife-obstetrician laborist teams, expanding the number of providers eligible to share laborist duties and reduce obstetrician burnout. In the second case, the hospital laborists refused to provide backup services to the midwives that was standardly provided to the obstetricians. These hospital constraints, in addition to hospital bylaws that require an obstetrician to cosign midwives’ documentation without statutory, regulatory, or reimbursement rationales, altogether disinhibit expansion and integration of midwifery in NV. Oregon’s path to eliminate these hospital discriminatory policies via legislative change is described below. MIDWIFERY CARE IN OR: A CASE STUDY In 2015, concerns of patient access and equity led OR midwives to advocate with state legislators and stakeholders to establish midwives' hospital admitting privileges and membership on medical staff with voting rights. This led to passage of law HB 2930 in 2015. The key motivation for this change stemmed from a lack of access to vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC) among patients at a federally qualified health center that provides care for migrant farmworkers and economically disadvantaged families. Patients seeking a VBAC were told they could not birth at their local hospital and had to travel at least 45 minutes to the academic medical center, despite the local hospital’s capacity to provide VBAC services per ACOG guidelines. The lead federally qualified health center perinatal clinician was a midwife who attended hospital medical staff meetings but was not allowed to vote or bring motions forward in that hospital system. Prior to passage of HB 2930, midwives managed a patient’s birth and postpartum care independently based on state licensure but without independent admitting privileges. Physician sign-off on all hospital admissions was required, which slowed care processes and routinely placed physicians at medicolegal risk. State- and hospital-level restrictions negatively impacted many rural counties in OR and contributed to perinatal care deserts. Informed by these concerns, local ACOG members gave testimony in support of midwifery independent admitting privileges, which led to support from the Oregon Medical Association and the Hospital Association of Oregon. SOLUTIONS TO INCREASING ACCESS, UTILIZATION, AND INFLUENCE OF MIDWIFERY CARE Several of the described state, federal, and hospital barriers contribute to midwifery burnout, tether the supply of midwives to physician demand instead of consumer demand for midwifery care, and limit the expansion and diversification of the midwifery workforce. When these barriers exist in combination, access to, utilization of, and the influence of midwifery care are exponentially halted. For example, in AL, Louisiana (LA), and Texas (TX), midwives simultaneously experience four critical barriers to caring for childbearing women: (1) invisibility in key perinatal data, (2) inequitable pay, (3) restrictive regulatory and legislative policies, and (4) discriminatory hospital policies. Alternatively, NM, OR, and the District of Columbia have independent midwifery practice regulations, equitable reimbursement, and laws against discriminatory hospital practices; collect the most accurate perinatal data; allow for autonomous prescription privileges; and permit midwives to independently admit their own patients to the hospital. The following 6 solutions are recommended to develop, sustain, and integrate the US midwifery workforce: Solution 1: Fund Midwifery Education and Compensate Preceptors State, federal, and health system funding streams should be developed in partnership with colleges and universities to launch and expand midwifery education programs. Increasing the number of midwifery education programs would exponentially grow the midwifery workforce. Increasing state and federal funding for scholarships, tuition support, and loan repayment programs would grow the midwifery workforce and expand access to midwifery care. Midwifery preceptors and/or health care systems should be compensated for their time to clinically train midwifery students, similar to Graduate Medical Education funding practices in medical education. One recent example of a successful midwifery education funding strategy is: the NJ Department of Health has provided $1 million per year over 3 years to support the NJ Midwifery Education Project within Rutgers University. Solution 2: Prioritize Local, State, and Federal Funding Initiatives That Increase Access to Midwifery Education Among Students of Color Recognizing the history of anti-Blackness and racism in the US health care system and to improve the birth care experience and outcomes of Black women, , efforts must be focused on diversifying the midwifery workforce via new funding streams and innovative pathways. Funding must focus on initiatives that promote the cultural, racial, and ethnic diversity of midwifery students. One solution is to support federal legislation, such as the federal Midwives for MOMS Act of 2023, which would increase the number of midwives from underrepresented groups. Development of midwifery education programs at historically Black colleges and universities would also increase the number of Black midwives. , Solution 3: Increase Attention to Reporting of Birth Data Solutions to addressing underreporting of midwifery-attended births are multifactorial and require an interprofessional approach. , Hospital leadership should examine and inform birth certificate data collection staff of potential systematic midwifery births miscoding as physician births and empower systems to prevent and eliminate vital statistics errors. Perinatal care providers should track their births, ensure they are accurately reported, and engage in quality assurance of their birth data. A monthly report could be distributed from each hospital to birth attendants for tracking. Regular birth registrar training should also occur, including, for example, the online training module with the National Center for Health Statistics. Solution 4: Advocate for Equitable Reimbursement One solution to supporting the expansion and integration of the midwifery workforce is mandating equitable private and Medicaid reimbursement rates for the same service in all 50 states. Parity in private insurance and Medicaid reimbursement will bolster and support the growth of midwifery care services, improve access to perinatal care, and help address rural health disparities and maternity care deserts.

Solution 5: Remove Legislative and Regulatory Restrictions of Midwifery Practice Physicians and midwives should advance coordinated advocacy to remove unnecessary legislative and regulatory restrictions, such as contractual or forced collaborative agreements, to licensure and prescriptive authority for midwives. Removal of legislative and regulatory restrictions promotes collaborative, complementary midwifery and physician care teams and allows midwives to better meet perinatal care needs. This solution can be directed either to leadership within a specific health care system or state legislative policy leaders. Interdisciplinary articulation of how these restrictions constrain both midwives and physicians is particularly informative to state legislators. Solution 6: Promote Unfettered Hospital Privileging and Full Medical Staff Autonomy Licensed midwives have all training necessary to safely and appropriately admit laboring patients to the hospital setting. All 50 states should follow exemplary state legislation in NM, OR, and the District of Columbia, which specifically protect the right of midwives to admit patients to the hospital. In addition, states should require that when hospitals grant midwives practice privileges this is accompanied with admitting privileges and membership on medical staff with voting rights. CONCLUSIONS The expansion and integration of midwives as part of the wider perinatal care workforce are common health system features of many countries with better perinatal health outcomes than in the United States. A myriad of restrictive US hospital, state, and federal practices and policies regarding midwifery training, reimbursement, licensing, prescribing, and admitting privileges create wide variations in use of midwives by state. These barriers must be addressed for the United States to incorporate midwifery care as a perinatal health systems solution. Extensive restrictions by state and federal government, health care organizations, and private insurance corporations constrain midwives’ ability to practice independently, often due to outdated practices or politics over sound policy. Many restrictions are due to the lack of awareness of the midwife’s education, licensure, skill set, care model, and/or scope of practice. Restrictions are also maintained via territorialism, abuse of power, purposeful inertia to retain current regulations, or active opposition to midwives practicing to their full capacity and being equitably paid. State legislation and regulation restrictions can significantly impact access to care, particularly when they limit midwives’ ability to practice. Working through the legislative and regulatory processes to create environments and health systems in which midwives can practice to the full extent of their training and licensure can maximize their workforce effort and expertise, thereby fostering an environment that improves access to care and perinatal outcomes. Legislation and policy changes are typically inspired by a problem in need of a solution. State and federal legislative, regulatory, and hospital restrictions to independent midwifery practice do not improve care; on the contrary, they worsen the existing crisis in perinatal care access and inequities and should be removed. Irrespective of the state, midwives should not be subjected to restrictions that run counter to the best available evidence, and obstetricians should not be pressured into collaborative relationships that elevate their vicarious liability or duplicate their work. Midwives are prepared to provide safe, autonomous perinatal care and collaborate with physician colleagues to increase access and use of perinatal care services and improve perinatal outcomes in the United States.
